thread.title: Amazon Earnings: How Much Better Can It Get?

author: Jon Swartz
title: Amazon Earnings: How Much Better Can It Get?
text:
By Jon Swartz Updated April 24, 2018 6:27 p.m. ET (Photo by David Ryder/Getty Images) Illustration: Getty Images The View From Silicon Valley
Neither the taunting tweets of President Donald Trump nor competition on all flanks is expected to slow Amazon.com (AMZN), which reports after the market closes on Thursday.
The e-commerce and cloud-computing juggernaut is expected to post first-quarter earnings of $1.26 per share on revenue of $49.88 billion, according to analysts polled by FactSet . In the same quarter a year ago, Amazon earned $1.48 on revenue of $35.7 billion.
Outsize expectations have become the baseline for Amazon, whose stock has vaulted 61% the past 12 months to $1,460.26.
"We expect continued topline momentum following a strong holiday season stemming from a healthy macro backdrop, record consumer sentiment levels, and the company’s expanding Prime membership base, which recently surpassed 100mm customers," Stifel analyst Scott Devitt said in a note.
Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos' letter to shareholders last week—disclosing for the first time that the $99-per-year Prime has more than 100 million paying subscribers worldwide—underscores the company's extraordinary reach. My colleague Alex Eule points out some 55% of the 126 million households in the U.S. subscribe to Prime.
The Seattle-based company's ambitions extend far beyond retail, and will soon be manifested in an army of robots and package deliveries to locked cars, among other ventures. In a partnership with General Motors (GM) and Volvo Cars , Amazon will deliver packages to the trunks of their cars in 37 U.S. cities for customers uncomfortable with packages left outside or couriers entering their homes.
Amazon's technological wave doesn't end there. It plans to unleash domestic robotic servants operating with the company’s Alexa voice-control system.
Expect Amazon's World Domination Tour to continue unabated into 2018 and beyond. The behemoth is expected to generate $3.37 billion in worldwide digital ads this year, about 1.2% of the market, up from 0.9% last year, forecasts eMarketer .
"Amazon’s success with Prime and continued investment in this part of the business shows that customer loyalty is more critical than ever," says Amit Sharma , CEO of Narvar , a post-purchase platform, who previously worked at Apple (AAPL) Walmart (WMT), and Williams-Sonoma (WSM).
So what could go wrong?
"I get nervous when you start getting stocks that are more than 20% [25% so far this year] above their 200-day moving averages, and that's exactly what you have with Amazon right now," Piper Jaffray Chief Market Technician Craig Johnson told CNBC. “You've got a divergence between the overall relative strength index and price. That suggests to me a little bit of an easing in momentum.”
Fellow FAANG member Netflix (NFLX), for example, reported sterling results last week yet struggled to nudge past its high of $333, Johnson said.
